analysis.cultural_economic_read: Low-density pastoral economy: extensive sheep and beef grazing on eroding soft-rock hill country, with exotic pine shelterbelts/woodlots and poplar-willow erosion control indicating land-management subsidy schemes. Infrastructure is minimal and aging — single-lane bridge, chip-seal one-lane road, timber guard rails, overhead single-phase distribution — a district council with a small rate base. Anglophone settler landscape (fenced paddocks, Pinus radiata, gorse/pampas weeds) with no visible settlement, shops or people; economically marginal back-country served mainly by farm traffic.

discriminators.title: One-lane bridge: NZ pictogram+blue arrow plate vs Australian worded sign
discriminators.body: In New Zealand a single-lane bridge is announced by a yellow diamond showing a black narrowing-bridge pictogram, usually with a blue rectangular plate carrying a large white arrow (your priority) and a small red opposing arrow. In Australia you would instead see a black-on-white or black-on-yellow worded 'ONE LANE BRIDGE' panel and a separate GIVE WAY arrangement without the blue arrow plate. Seeing the blue arrow-priority plate essentially settles NZ.

discriminators.title: Papa mudstone cut banks mark eastern North Island, not South Island greywacke
discriminators.body: Eastern North Island backroads cut into soft, pale grey-white Tertiary papa mudstone that rills and slumps into rounded, tree-free hill faces. In the South Island you would instead see hard angular greywacke or schist cuts, braided shingle riverbeds and Nothofagus beech forest. A silty, single-channel stream in a steep incised gully with willows reinforces the North Island reading.

discriminators.title: Drought-browned pasture with green gullies = eastern rain shadow, not Taranaki/Waikato
discriminators.body: On the rain-shadowed eastern North Island, midsummer hill pasture is fully straw-brown while only the gully bottoms stay green, and cut banks are chalky pale grey. In Taranaki or Waikato you would instead see pasture staying green through summer and road cuts exposing dark brown andesitic ash and tephra layers. Combine this with poplar erosion plantings to confirm the eastern papa belt.

discriminators.title: Toetoe plumes and broadleaf bush vs eucalypt woodland
discriminators.body: New Zealand rural roadsides mix dense dark broadleaf bush, flax and cabbage-tree forms, tall toetoe/pampas plumes and exotic Pinus radiata shelterbelts. In comparable Australian hill country you would instead see open eucalypt woodland with stringybark or gum trunks, sparse understorey and no toetoe plumes. The absence of any eucalypt silhouette on a left-hand-drive-free, left-traffic road strongly favours NZ.
